title: Agents That Learn on the Job Without Weight Updates
hook: An agent that cracks a hard request today starts from zero tomorrow. Distil each episode into a retrievable rule and a frozen model gets 2.6x better — no fine-tuning.
key_points: Frozen deployed models discard the feedback ordinary operation already produces: outcome verdicts and after-the-fact corrections.
Pairs the frozen model with an external memory that distils each episode into retrievable natural-language rules.
On tau-bench's banking domain, learning from just the one-bit outcome verdict lifts single-trial success to 1.6x the static-RAG baseline.
Learning from corrections reaches 2.6x, solving 22 of the 84 tasks the baseline never solves.
Holds on Mistral Large (self-hostable open weights) and replicates on a frontier model, Claude Sonnet 5.
The memory transfers between models: each one reading the store built by the other beats its own no-memory baseline.
content_html: Tablan, Taylor, and Bernhem start from a waste observation: an AI agent meets learning opportunities in every episode and throws nearly all of them away, because the model is frozen at deployment. Solve a hard request today and the agent begins from scratch when it recurs tomorrow. Yet ordinary operation already emits usable feedback — outcome verdicts and after-the-fact corrections. Their claim is that this feedback suffices for continual learning if you pair the frozen model with an external memory that distils each episode into retrievable natural-language rules.
extra_html:
The numbers

On the banking domain of τ-bench, measured against a static-RAG control that retrieves over the complete policy corpus, learning from the one-bit outcome verdict alone lifts single-trial success to 1.6× the baseline, and learning from corrections reaches 2.6×. That converts 22 of the 84 tasks the baseline never solves. The result spans the deployment spectrum: it holds on Mistral Large — open weights that organisations with data-sovereignty requirements can self-host — and replicates on a frontier model, Claude Sonnet 5.

Why the transfer result matters

The accumulated memory is not model-specific. Each model reading the store built by the other rose above its own no-memory baseline, which suggests the rules capture genuine task knowledge rather than one model's idiosyncrasies — and hints that such a store could outlive the model that produced it. The authors release the harness, protocol, and data.

related.title: Do Agent Optimizers Compound? A Continual-Learning Evaluation
related.hook: Most agent-optimization papers report a one-shot gain and stop. Rerun the optimizer on new tasks and two of three popular methods actually make the agent worse than doing nothing.

related.title: Agentic Test-Time Training: Adapting Mid-Episode
related.hook: LLM agents degrade over long episodes, repeating failed moves — this method updates the model's weights continuously during the episode itself, but only on genuinely new information.

flashcards.prompt: How can an agent keep improving when the underlying model's weights are frozen at deployment?
flashcards.back_html: By writing to an external memory instead of the weights: each episode is distilled into retrievable natural-language rules that later runs read back, so yesterday's solved request informs tomorrow's.

flashcards.prompt: Which feedback signal produced the larger gain in this study?

choices.text: After-the-fact corrections (2.6x baseline) beat the one-bit outcome verdict (1.6x)
The one-bit outcome verdict, because it is available on every single episode
Both landed at the same multiple — the signal's content didn't matter, only its presence

flashcards.explanation_html: Richer feedback helped more, but the striking part is that even a single bit of outcome verdict was enough to lift success to 1.6x the static-RAG control.

flashcards.prompt: What does it mean that the accumulated memory 'transfers' across models?
flashcards.back_html: Each model reading the rule store built by the other model rose above its own no-memory baseline — so what the memory captures is reusable knowledge, not quirks of one model.
